source_text: Deleant igitur et testimonia daemonum filium David proclamantia Iesum, sed testimonia apostolorum delere non poterunt, si daemonum indigna sunt. Ipse inprimis Matthaeus, fidelissimus evangelii commentator, ut comes domini, non aliam ob causam quam ut nos originis Christi carnalis compotes faceret ita exorsus est: Liber geniturae Iesu Christi, filii David, filii Abraham. His originis fontibus genere manante cum gradatim ordo deducitur ad Christi nativitatem, quid aliud quam caro ipsa Abrahae et David per singulos traducem sui faciens in virginem usque describitur inferens Christum, immo ipse Christus producitur de virgine? Sed et Paulus, utpote eiusdem evangelii et discipulus et magister et testis, qua eiusdem ipsius Christi apostolus, confirmat Christum ex semine David secundum carnem, utique ipsius. Ergo ex semine David caro Christi. Si secundum Mariae carnem ex semine David, ergo ex Mariae carne est, dum ex semine est David. Quocunque detorseris dictum, aut ex carne est Mariae quod ex semine est David, aut ex David semine est quod ex carne est Mariae. Totam hanc controversiam dirimit idem apostolus, ipsum definiens esse Abrahae semen. Cum Abraham, utique multo magis David, quasi recentioris. Retexens enim promissionem benedictionis nationum in nomine Abraham, Et in semine tuo benedicentur omnes nationes, Non, inquit, dixit seminibus, tanquam de pluribus, sed semine, de uno, quod est Christus. Qui haec legimus et credimus, quam debemus et possumus agnoscere in Christo carnis qualitatem? utique non aliam quam Abraham, siquidem semen Abra ham Christus; nec aliam quam Iesse, siquidem ex radice Iesse flos Christus; nec aliam, quam David, siquidem fructus ex lumbis David Christus; nec aliam quam ex Maria, siquidem ex Mariae utero Christus; et adhuc superius nec aliam quam Adam, siquidem secundus Adam Christus. Consequens ergo est ut aut illos spiritalem carnem habuisse contendant, quo eadem conditio substantiae deducatur in Christo, aut concedant carnem Christi spiritalem non fuisse, quae non de spiritali stirpe censetur.
thought_title: Christ's flesh traced through the seed of David and Abraham
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christ's flesh is ordinary human flesh because Scripture traces his descent through Mary from David, Abraham, Jesse, and Adam.
pass_a_gloss: Let them therefore blot out also the testimonies of the demons proclaiming Jesus son of David, but the testimonies of the apostles they will not be able to blot out, if the testimonies of the demons are unworthy. Matthew himself first of all, the most faithful commentator of the gospel, as companion of the Lord, for no other reason than that he might make us sharers in the carnal origin of Christ, began thus: The book of the birth of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Since from these fountains of origin the race flows and the order is traced step by step down to the birth of Christ, what else is described than the very flesh of Abraham and David, making a transmission of itself through each one down to the virgin, bringing in Christ, or rather Christ himself is brought forth from the virgin? But Paul also, as both disciple and teacher and witness of the same gospel, as apostle of that same Christ himself, confirms that Christ is from the seed of David according to the flesh, that is, of David himself. Therefore from the seed of David is the flesh of Christ. If according to the flesh of Mary from the seed of David, therefore it is from the flesh of Mary, since it is from the seed of David. Whichever way you twist the saying, either what is from the seed of David is from the flesh of Mary, or what is from the flesh of Mary is from the seed of David. This whole controversy the same apostle settles, defining that he himself is the seed of Abraham. Since Abraham, certainly much more David, as more recent. For unrolling the promise of the blessing of the nations in the name of Abraham, And in your seed all nations will be blessed, He did not, he says, say seeds, as of many, but seed, of one, which is Christ. We who read and believe these things, what quality of flesh ought we and can we recognize in Christ? Certainly not other than Abraham, since indeed Christ is the seed of Abraham; nor other than Jesse, since indeed Christ is the flower from the root of Jesse; nor other than David, since indeed Christ is the fruit from the loins of David; nor other than from Mary, since indeed Christ is from the womb of Mary; and still higher up, nor other than Adam, since indeed Christ is the second Adam. It follows therefore that either they must contend that those men had spiritual flesh, so that the same condition of substance may be traced down into Christ, or they must concede that the flesh of Christ was not spiritual, which is not reckoned from a spiritual stock.

lemmas.gloss: may be traced down, may be led down

choices.why: The adjective modifies origin; 'carnal' keeps the flesh-root visible and matches the glossary's flesh vocabulary.
The glossary requires 'birth' for nativitas; genitura is the same root and refers to the genealogy of Christ's birth.
Tradux means a shoot or transmission; the phrase describes flesh passing itself down through generations.
Dirimo means to separate or settle a dispute; 'settles' fits the legal tone of the controversy.
Stirps means root or lineage; 'stock' preserves the botanical metaphor alongside root and flower.

pass_b_english: Let them then erase the testimonies of the demons that proclaim Jesus the Son of David, but they will not be able to erase the testimonies of the apostles, if the demons' testimonies are unworthy. Matthew himself first of all, the most faithful commentator on the gospel, as the Lord's companion, began for no other reason than to make us sharers in the carnal origin of Christ: "The book of the birth of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Since the order is traced step by step down to Christ's birth from these fountains of origin, with his lineage flowing on, what else is described but the very flesh of Abraham and David making a transmission of itself through each generation down to the virgin, bringing Christ in—indeed, Christ himself is brought forth from the virgin? But Paul too, as both disciple and teacher and witness of the same gospel, as apostle of that same Christ, confirms that Christ is from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3)—his own flesh, of course. Therefore Christ's flesh is from the seed of David. If it is from the seed of David according to Mary's flesh, then it is from Mary's flesh, since it is from David's seed. Whichever way you twist the saying, either what is from David's seed is from Mary's flesh, or what is from Mary's flesh is from David's seed. The same apostle settles this whole controversy by defining Christ himself as the seed of Abraham. Since he is Abraham's seed, much more is he David's, as the more recent. For unrolling the promise of blessing for the nations in Abraham's name—"And in your seed all nations will be blessed"—he says, "He did not say 'seeds,' as of many, but 'seed,' of one, which is Christ" (Galatians 3:16). We who read and believe these things, what quality of flesh ought we—and can we—recognize in Christ? Certainly none other than Abraham's, since Christ is the seed of Abraham; none other than Jesse's, since Christ is the flower from Jesse's root; none other than David's, since Christ is the fruit from David's loins; none other than Mary's, since Christ is from Mary's womb; and still further back, none other than Adam's, since Christ is the second Adam. It follows therefore that either they must maintain that those men had spiritual flesh, so that the same condition of substance may be traced down into Christ, or they must concede that Christ's flesh was not spiritual, since it is not reckoned from spiritual stock.
